1.solution: Let \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}=\vec{C}\), with angle \(\theta\) between \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\). When \(\vec{B}\) is doubled, the new resultant \(\vec{C_1}=\vec{A}+2\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\). The component of \(\vec{A}+2\vec{B}\) along \(\vec{A}\) must vanish: \(A+2B\cos\theta=0\), so \(A=-2B\cos\theta\). Now \(C^2=A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta\). Note \(2AB\cos\theta=A\cdot(2B\cos\theta)=A\cdot(-A)=-A^2\). Hence \(C^2=A^2+B^2-A^2=B^2\), giving \(C=B\).

2.solution: For a real, inverted image twice the object size, magnification \(m=\dfrac{v}{u}=-2\), so \(v=-2u\). Lens formula: \(\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{v}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{-2u}-\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{-3}{2u}\). With \(f=\dfrac{1}{3}\,m\): \(u=-\dfrac{3}{2}f=-\dfrac{3}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}=-0.5\,m\). The object distance is \(0.5\,m\).

3.solution: A tuning fork resonates only with a fork whose frequency is an integral multiple (harmonic) of its own. \(512=2\times256\) and \(768=3\times256\) are harmonics, and \(256\,Hz\) is identical. But \(754\,Hz\) is not an integral multiple of \(256\,Hz\), so it will not resonate with the \(256\,Hz\) fork.

4.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
4.solution: A charge rotating once per second is an effective current \(I=\dfrac{q}{t}=1000e\). The field at the centre of the circular path is \(B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}\). Given \(B=x\mu_0\): \(x\mu_0=\dfrac{\mu_0(1000e)}{2r}\), so \(r=\dfrac{1000e}{2x}=\dfrac{1000\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{2\times(2\times10^{-16})}=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-16}}{4\times10^{-16}}=0.4\,m\).

5.subtopic: Circular Motion — Angular Velocity, Centripetal Force, Vertical Circle
5.solution: Frequency \(f=\dfrac{x}{t}\) and radius \(r=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\,m\). Tangential velocity \(v=\omega r=2\pi f r=2\pi\times\dfrac{x}{t}\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{\pi^2 x}{t}\).

6.solution: In Bohr's model \(v_n\propto\dfrac{1}{n}\) and \(r_n\propto n^2\). The frequency of revolution \(f=\dfrac{v_n}{2\pi r_n}\propto\dfrac{1/n}{n^2}=\dfrac{1}{n^3}\). Hence \(f\) is inversely proportional to \(n^3\).

7.solution: Rise in temperature \(\Delta T=T_2-T_1=82.3-38.6=43.7^{\circ}C\). For a difference, absolute errors add: \(\Delta(\delta T)=0.2+0.3=0.5\). Hence \(\Delta T=(43.7\pm0.5)^{\circ}C\).

8.solution: Terminal velocity \(v\propto r^2\). For the small drops \(V\propto r^2\) and for the big drop \(v_b\propto R^2\). Dividing: \(\dfrac{v_b}{V}=\dfrac{R^2}{r^2}\), so \(v_b=\dfrac{VR^2}{r^2}\).

9.solution: For a spring-mass system \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}\), so \(\dfrac{m}{k}=\dfrac{T^2}{4\pi^2}=\dfrac{36}{4\pi^2}=\dfrac{9}{\pi^2}\). At rest, \(mg=kx\), so the static stretch \(x=\dfrac{m}{k}g=\dfrac{9}{\pi^2}\times\pi^2=9\,m\) (using \(g=\pi^2=10\)).

11.subtopic: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws — Induced EMF, Current, and Charge
11.solution: Lenz's law states that the induced current opposes the change in flux that produces it. This opposition requires work to be done against the induced effect, which is exactly what conserves energy. Thus Lenz's law in induction is a direct consequence of the conservation of energy.

12.solution: From the circuit: A passes through a NOT gate giving \(X=\overline{A}\); B and C pass through a NAND gate giving \(Z=\overline{B\cdot C}\); X and Z feed an OR gate: \(Y=\overline{A}+\overline{B\cdot C}\). When all inputs are LOW \((A=B=C=0)\): \(Y=1+1=1\). When all inputs are HIGH \((A=B=C=1)\): \(Y=0+0=0\). Hence the outputs are \((1,0)\).

13.subtopic: Average KE, Equipartition, and Specific Heats
13.solution: Average kinetic energy of a molecule \(\propto T\). Therefore \(\dfrac{(KE)_B}{(KE)_A}=\dfrac{T_B}{T_A}=\dfrac{420}{350}=\dfrac{6}{5}\), i.e. \(6:5\).

14.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
14.solution: In S.H.M. the restoring force \(F=-m\omega^2 y\), so force and displacement are exactly out of phase (phase difference \(\pi\)). The given displacement-time graph rises to a positive peak first; the force-time graph must therefore start by going negative (the inverted curve). This is option (C).

16.solution: The sphere enters the liquid with speed \(u=\sqrt{2gh}\). Inside the liquid (\(\sigma>\rho\)) the net upward force gives deceleration \(a=\dfrac{(\sigma-\rho)g}{\rho}\). It stops when \(v=0\): \(0=u^2-2aH\), so \(H=\dfrac{u^2}{2a}=\dfrac{2gh}{2\,(\sigma-\rho)g/\rho}=\dfrac{h\rho}{\sigma-\rho}\). The intended option is \(\dfrac{h\rho}{(\rho-\sigma)}\) (option D, denominator written with reversed sign; magnitude \(=\dfrac{h\rho}{\sigma-\rho}\)).

17.solution: Thermal resistances in series: \(R_1=\dfrac{x}{KA}\), \(R_2=\dfrac{4x}{2KA}=\dfrac{2x}{KA}\), so \(R_{eq}=\dfrac{3x}{KA}\). Rate of heat flow \(\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=\dfrac{T_2-T_1}{R_{eq}}=\dfrac{KA(T_2-T_1)}{3x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\dfrac{A(T_2-T_1)K}{x}\right]\). Hence \(f=\dfrac{1}{3}\).

18.subtopic: Pipes, Resonance Tube, and Doppler Effect
18.solution: A pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics. Its overtones are \(3n, 5n, 7n\) (first, second, third overtones), where \(n\) is the fundamental. Given \(3n+5n+7n=15n=3930\), so \(n=262\,Hz\).

20.subtopic: Projectile Motion — Range, Height, and Time of Flight
20.solution: Initial KE \(E=\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2\). At the highest point only the horizontal velocity \(u\cos\theta\) remains. So KE there \(=\dfrac{1}{2}m(u\cos\theta)^2=\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2\cos^2\theta=E\cos^2\theta\).

21.subtopic: Young's Double Slit, Biprism, and Interference
21.solution: Intensity \(I=4I_0\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}\) where \(\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta x\). For \(\Delta x=\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), \(\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(I=4I_0\cos^2\dfrac{\pi}{4}=2I_0=\dfrac{K}{2}\), giving \(K=4I_0\). For \(\Delta x=\lambda\), \(\phi=2\pi\), so \(I=4I_0\cos^2\pi=4I_0=K\).

22.subtopic: Magnetisation, Susceptibility, Permeability, and B-H-M Relations
22.solution: The net magnetic field inside a material is the sum of the applied field and the field due to magnetisation: \(B=\mu_0(H+M)\).

24.subtopic: de Broglie Wavelength and Matter Waves
24.solution: For an accelerated electron, \(\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}\). Hence \(\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda}=\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{9V}}=\dfrac{1}{3}\), so \(\lambda_2=\dfrac{\lambda}{3}\).

25.subtopic: Circular Motion — Angular Velocity, Centripetal Force, Vertical Circle
25.solution: Maximum tension \(T_{max}=3.7\,kg\,wt=3.7\times10=37\,N\). At the lowest point of a vertical circle the tension is maximum: \(T_{max}=mg+m\omega^2 r\). With \(m=0.5\,kg\), \(r=4\,m\): \(37=0.5\times10+0.5\times\omega^2\times4=5+2\omega^2\). So \(2\omega^2=32\), \(\omega^2=16\), \(\omega=4\,rad/s\).

26.subtopic: Viscosity, Stokes' Law, Terminal Velocity, and Reynolds
26.solution: For steady (laminar) flow with velocity increasing linearly from the bed, \(\dfrac{v}{h}\) is constant: \(\dfrac{v_A}{h_A}=\dfrac{v_B}{h_B}\). With \(v_A=12\,cm/s\), \(h_A=40\,cm\), \(h_B=90\,cm\): \(v_B=v_A\times\dfrac{h_B}{h_A}=12\times\dfrac{90}{40}=27\,cm/s\).

27.solution: Wavelength \(\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}=\dfrac{336}{400}=0.84\,m\). A phase difference of \(60^{\circ}\) corresponds to a path difference \(\dfrac{60}{360}\lambda=\dfrac{\lambda}{6}\). So separation \(=\dfrac{0.84}{6}=0.14\,m\).

29.solution: Bohr quantisation: \(mvR=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\) ... (i). For motion in a transverse field, \(qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow mvR=\dfrac{qBR^2}{1}\)... eliminating, from (i) \(R=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi mv}\). Using \(qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{R}\Rightarrow qBR=mv\), combine with (i): \(qBR\cdot R=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\Rightarrow qBR^2=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\). Energy \(E=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2=\dfrac{1}{2}qBvR\). Since \(mv=qBR\) and \(mvR=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\Rightarrow vR=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi m}\). Thus \(E=\dfrac{1}{2}qB\,vR=\dfrac{1}{2}qB\cdot\dfrac{nh}{2\pi m}=\dfrac{nqBh}{4\pi m}\). For \(n=2\): \(E=\dfrac{qBh}{2\pi m}\).

30.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
30.solution: For a body, \(a+r+t_r=1\) (absorption + reflection + transmission coefficients). So \(t_r=1-(0.77+0.17)=0.06\). Heat transmitted \(=t_r\times Q=0.06\times250=15\,kcal\).

31.solution: First minimum from centre: \(y_1=\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}\). Distance between the two first minima on either side: \(2y_1=\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\). So \(1\times10^{-2}=\dfrac{2\lambda\times2}{0.2\times10^{-3}}\), giving \(\lambda=\dfrac{(1\times10^{-2})(0.2\times10^{-3})}{4}=5\times10^{-7}\,m=5000\,\text{ angstrom}\).

32.solution: \(\dfrac{L}{R}\) has the unit \(\dfrac{\text{henry}}{\text{ohm}}\). The time constant of an LR circuit is \(\tau=\dfrac{L}{R}\), which has the SI unit of second.

33.subtopic: Power in AC Circuit — Average, Factor, Wattless
33.solution: Impedance \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}=\sqrt{R^2+3R^2}=2R\). Average power \(P=\dfrac{E_0}{\sqrt2}\cdot\dfrac{E_0}{\sqrt2 Z}\cdot\cos\phi\) with \(\cos\phi=\dfrac{R}{Z}=\dfrac{1}{2}\). So \(P=\dfrac{E_0^2}{2(2R)}\times\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{E_0^2}{8R}\).

34.solution: Force \(F=qE\), acceleration \(a=\dfrac{qE}{m}\), starting from rest \(v=at=\dfrac{qEt}{m}\). KE \(=\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2=\dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{qEt}{m}\right)^2=\dfrac{q^2E^2t^2}{2m}\).

35.solution: Internal resistance \(r=R\left(\dfrac{l}{l_1}-1\right)\), where \(l\) is the open-circuit balancing length. So \(5\left(\dfrac{l}{250}-1\right)=20\left(\dfrac{l}{400}-1\right)\). This gives \(\dfrac{l}{50}-5=\dfrac{l}{20}-20\Rightarrow15=\dfrac{3l}{100}\Rightarrow l=500\,cm\). Then \(r=5\left(\dfrac{500}{250}-1\right)=5\,\Omega\).

36.subtopic: Rotational Kinetic Energy and Rolling Motion
36.solution: Sliding (no rotation): \(V=\sqrt{2gh}\). Rolling: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1+K^2/R^2}}\). For a ring \(K^2/R^2=1\), so \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2gh}}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{V}{\sqrt2}\).

37.solution: Initial parallel combination: \(C_i=C+C=2C\). After filling one capacitor with dielectric \(K\): \(C_f=C+KC=C(1+K)\). Change \(\Delta C=C(1+K)-2C=C(K-1)\).

38.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation
38.solution: Using \(PV=nRT\) at constant T,V: before, \(n_1=\dfrac{PV}{RT}\); after, \(n_2=\dfrac{P'V}{RT}\). Moles leaked \(=n_1-n_2=\dfrac{V}{RT}(P-P')\).
38.note: Stem uses P' for the reduced pressure (printed as 'P' twice due to extraction); option B = V/RT (P - P').

39.subtopic: Gravitational PE, Escape Velocity, and Energy
39.solution: Escape velocity \(v_e=\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\) depends on \(G\), the mass \(M\) of the earth and its radius \(R\), but not on the mass of the projected object.

40.subtopic: p-n Junction Diode — Biasing, I-V, and Rectifiers
40.solution: In an unbiased p-n junction, diffusion leaves the depletion region with negative ions on the p-side and positive ions on the n-side, creating a built-in field directed from the n-side to the p-side. The n-side is at higher potential than the p-side.

42.subtopic: Ohm's Law, Cells, EMF, and Internal Resistance
42.solution: Two equal cells in series: \(I=\dfrac{2E}{R+r_1+r_2}\). Terminal p.d. across cell \(E_1\): \(V_1=E-Ir_1=0\). So \(E=\dfrac{2E\,r_1}{R+r_1+r_2}\Rightarrow R+r_1+r_2=2r_1\Rightarrow R=r_1-r_2\).

43.subtopic: SHM Energy — Kinetic, Potential, and Total
43.solution: Total energy \(E=\dfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2\) with amplitude \(A\) fixed. For a pendulum \(\omega^2=\dfrac{g}{l}\), so \(E\propto\dfrac{1}{l}\). Reducing \(l\) to \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) makes \(E\) three times larger.

44.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
44.subtopic: Force on Current-Carrying Conductor and Parallel Wires
44.solution: Force per length between parallel wires \(F\propto\dfrac{I_1 I_2}{d}\). Initially attractive (same direction): \(F=k\dfrac{I_1 I_2}{d}\). After increasing separation to \(3d\) the force becomes repulsive of magnitude \(\dfrac{2}{3}F\): \(\dfrac{2}{3}\,k\dfrac{I_1 I_2}{d}=k\dfrac{I_1' I_2}{3d}\). Solving for the magnitude: \(|I_1'|=2I_1\). A repulsive force requires the currents to be antiparallel, i.e. the direction is reversed. So the current must be made twice and reversed.

45.subtopic: Transistors — BJT, CE Amplifier, and Gain

46.subtopic: First Law, Internal Energy, and Work-Heat Relations
46.solution: At constant pressure \(\Delta Q=nC_p\Delta T\), \(\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T\). Fraction into internal energy \(\dfrac{\Delta U}{\Delta Q}=\dfrac{C_v}{C_p}=\dfrac{1}{\gamma}\). For a monoatomic gas \(\gamma=\dfrac{5}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{\Delta U}{\Delta Q}=\dfrac{3}{5}=60\%\) (A) and external work \(=40\%\) (B). Hence \(A:B=60:40=3:2\).

47.subtopic: Power in AC Circuit — Average, Factor, Wattless
47.solution: LR circuit power factor \(X_1=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}}=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+9R^2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\). Adding \(X_C=R\) gives an LCR circuit: \(X_2=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}}=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2+(3R-R)^2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\). Ratio \(\dfrac{X_1}{X_2}=\dfrac{1/\sqrt{10}}{1/\sqrt5}=\dfrac{\sqrt5}{\sqrt{10}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\), i.e. \(1:\sqrt2\).

48.solution: On a sonometer \(f\propto\dfrac{1}{l}\). The shorter length (0.69 m) gives the higher frequency. Beat frequency \(f_2-f_1=6\). With \(\dfrac{f_1}{f_2}=\dfrac{l_2}{l_1}=\dfrac{0.69}{0.70}\), solving \(f_1\cdot0.70=f_2\cdot0.69\) with \(f_2-f_1=6\) gives \(f_1=414\,Hz\) and \(f_2=420\,Hz\).

50.solution: A point exactly in front of one slit is at \(y=\dfrac{d}{2}\). The \(n\)th minimum lies at \(y_n=\dfrac{(2n-1)\lambda D}{2d}\). For the 3rd minimum \((n=3)\): \(\dfrac{d}{2}=\dfrac{5\lambda D}{2d}\Rightarrow\lambda=\dfrac{d^2}{5D}\). 53.solution: Reduction of a nitrile with stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid gives an aldimine salt, which on acid hydrolysis yields an aldehyde. This is the Stephen reaction.\n\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}\equiv\text{N} \xrightarrow{\text{SnCl}_2,\,\text{HCl}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{NH}\cdot\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CHO}\) (benzaldehyde).

54.subtopic: Types of Solutions, Solubility and Henry's Law
54.solution: The dissolution of \(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\) in water is exothermic. By Le Chatelier's principle, for an exothermic dissolution an increase in temperature shifts the equilibrium back towards the undissolved solid, so its solubility decreases as temperature rises. The other salts (NaBr, NaCl, \(\text{NaNO}_3\)) show increasing solubility with temperature.

55.solution: Nylon 6,6 is formed by condensation polymerization of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid with elimination of water. Polythene, polyacrylonitrile and Teflon are all addition (chain-growth) polymers.

56.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
56.solution: Since \(E^{\circ}(\text{Zn}^{2+}\mid\text{Zn})=-0.76\,\text{V} < E^{\circ}(\text{H}^+\mid\text{H}_2)=0\,\text{V}\), zinc is the anode (negative electrode) and the hydrogen electrode is the cathode (positive electrode). At the positive electrode reduction occurs: \(2\text{H}^+_{(aq)}+2e^- \to \text{H}_{2(g)}\).

57.solution: Fibres are polymers with high tensile strength and strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding that can be drawn into threads. Nylon 6,6 is a polyamide fibre. Urea-formaldehyde resin is a thermosetting plastic, polystyrene is a thermoplastic, and neoprene is an elastomer.

58.subtopic: Rate of Reaction, Stoichiometry and Average Rate
58.solution: For \(\text{N}_2+3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3\), the rate in terms of reactants (which are consumed, so their concentration changes are negative) and products is:\n\(\text{Rate}=-\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2]}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\text{H}_2]}{dt}=+\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{NH}_3]}{dt}\). Option C states exactly this.

59.subtopic: Industrial Processes, Minerals, Hydrogen Compounds and Alloys
59.solution: Very pure dihydrogen (greater than 99.5 percent) is obtained by the electrolysis of a warm aqueous solution of barium hydroxide using nickel electrodes. The other methods give hydrogen contaminated with other gases.

60.subtopic: Reactions of Alkenes, Addition, Oxidation and Ozonolysis
60.solution: Hot acidic \(\text{KMnO}_4\) (in dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)) carries out oxidative cleavage of the ring double bond of cyclohexene. The ring opens and both alkene carbons are oxidised to carboxylic acid groups, giving a six-carbon dicarboxylic acid, \(\text{HOOC-(CH}_2)_4\text{-COOH}\), which is adipic acid (hexanedioic acid).

61.subtopic: Thermochemistry, Hess's Law and Bond Enthalpy
61.solution: Moles of benzene \(=\dfrac{13}{78}=0.1667\,\text{mol}\). This requires 5.1 kJ for vaporisation.\nEnthalpy of vaporisation per mole \(=\dfrac{5.1}{0.1667}=30.6\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Volume occupied by the single particle \(=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\dfrac{a^3}{8}\).\nWith unit-cell volume \(a^3 = x\times 10^{-23}\,\text{cm}^3\) and particle volume \(=2.1\times 10^{-23}\,\text{cm}^3\):\n\(2.1\times 10^{-23} = \dfrac{4}{3}\times\dfrac{22}{7}\times\dfrac{x\times 10^{-23}}{8}\), giving \(x = \dfrac{2.1\times 3\times 7\times 8}{4\times 22} = 4.0\).

63.subtopic: IUPAC and Common Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
63.solution: The structure is a cyclobutane ring bearing an \(-\text{OCH}_3\) (methoxy) group on one carbon and two methyl groups (gem-dimethyl) on the opposite carbon. The substituents are named alphabetically and the locant set is chosen as the lowest: the gem-dimethyl carbon is C1 and the methoxy carbon is C3, giving \(\{1,1,3\}\). Hence the IUPAC name is 3-methoxy-1,1-dimethylcyclobutane.
63.note: Stem figure (image11) read: cyclobutane with O-CH3 at top carbon and gem-dimethyl at the opposite carbon.

64.solution: Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer:\n\(\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = 4.680+\log_{10}\dfrac{0.02}{0.01} = 4.680+0.301 = 4.981\).

65.solution: The heat released to the surroundings is \(525\,\text{kJ}\), so for the surroundings \(q_{surr}=+525\,\text{kJ}\) at \(T=300\,\text{K}\).\n\(\Delta S_{surr}=-\dfrac{\Delta H_{sys}}{T}=\dfrac{525\times 10^3}{300}=1750\,\text{J K}^{-1}\).

66.subtopic: IUPAC Nomenclature, Functional Groups and Homologous Series
66.solution: Neopentane is 2,2-dimethylpropane: a central carbon bonded to four methyl groups, \(\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_4\). In bond-line notation this is drawn as four lines radiating from a single central point (an X/star shape). Option C shows exactly this four-bonds-from-one-centre structure, so it is neopentane.
66.note: All four options are structure images (image12-15). Option C (image14, X-shape) is neopentane = 2,2-dimethylpropane. | Backfill 2026-06-26: was describe-as-text (option text named the answer =neopentane, a giveaway); re-attached the 4 structure figures + neutral labels.

67.solution: The reduction is \(2\text{H}^+ + 2e^- \to \text{H}_2\). Forming 1 mole of \(\text{H}_2\) requires 2 moles of electrons. Since \(1\,F = 1\) mole of electrons, 2 faraday are required.

68.solution: The figure shows a vertical and a horizontal line crossing at the chiral carbon, with the vertical chain (COOH up, CH3 down) drawn as going away from the viewer and the horizontal groups (H, OH) coming towards the viewer. This is the Fischer projection formula.
68.note: Stem figure (image16) read: cross with COOH (top), CH3 (bottom), H (left), OH (right) = Fischer projection.

69.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
69.solution: Oleum (fuming sulphuric acid) is formed by absorbing \(\text{SO}_3\) in concentrated sulphuric acid: \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{SO}_3 \to \text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7\) (pyrosulphuric acid). Its molecular formula is \(\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7\).

70.subtopic: Balancing Redox Reactions and Oxidized/Reduced Species
70.solution: A redox reaction involves a change in oxidation numbers. In \(\text{Zn}+2\text{AgCN} \to 2\text{Ag}+\text{Zn(CN)}_2\), zinc goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised) and silver goes from +1 to 0 (reduced). The other three are double-displacement/acid-base reactions with no change in oxidation state.

71.subtopic: Preparation Methods of Aldehydes and Ketones
71.solution: Methylmagnesium bromide with \(\text{CdCl}_2\) forms dimethylcadmium, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Cd}\) (product A). Dialkylcadmium reagents react with acyl chlorides to give ketones: \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{Cd}+2\text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \to 2\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3\). The product B is propanone (acetone).

72.solution: Linolenic acid is 9,12,15-octadecatrienoic acid; the prefix 'trien' indicates three carbon-carbon double bonds. Hence it contains three \(>\!\text{C}=\text{C}\!<\) bonds.

73.solution: In an allylic halide the halogen is on an \(sp^3\) carbon directly adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond. 3-Bromopropene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{Br}\), has Br on the \(sp^3\) carbon next to the C=C, so it is allylic. (1- and 2-bromopropene are vinylic; 4-bromobut-1-ene is homoallylic.)

74.solution: Heating an alkyl bromide with silver fluoride replaces bromine by fluorine (Swarts reaction). tert-Butyl bromide, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}\), gives \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CF}\), which is 2-fluoro-2-methylpropane.

75.solution: \(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0 = 319.8 - 319.5 = 0.3\,\text{K}\).\nFrom \(\Delta T_b = K_b\,m\): \(K_b = \dfrac{\Delta T_b}{m} = \dfrac{0.3}{0.12} = 2.5\,\text{K kg mol}^{-1}\), which is option C.
75.note: AK key is B (3.0) but its own worked solution derives 2.5 K kg mol^-1, which is option C. 0.3/0.12 = 2.5 exactly. Correct answer is C; AK key letter is a transcription error.

76.subtopic: Glycosidic Linkages in Di- and Polysaccharides
76.solution: Both sucrose and lactose are disaccharides that release exactly one mole of glucose per mole on hydrolysis: sucrose \(\to\) glucose + fructose; lactose \(\to\) glucose + galactose. Maltose gives two glucose, and raffinose is a trisaccharide, so they do not match. Hence the pair giving equal (one each) glucose is sucrose and lactose.

77.solution: A molecule has a regular (expected) geometry only when the central atom has no lone pairs, so the electron-pair geometry and molecular geometry coincide. \(\text{SiCl}_4\) has four bond pairs and no lone pairs, giving a regular tetrahedral shape. \(\text{SF}_4\) (see-saw), \(\text{BrF}_5\) (square pyramidal) and \(\text{XeF}_4\) (square planar) all have lone pairs that distort the geometry.

78.solution: In the Hofmann bromamide degradation, an amide \(\text{R-CONH}_2\) is converted to a primary amine \(\text{R-NH}_2\) with one fewer carbon, effectively losing a CO group. The mass of CO is \(12+16 = 28\), so the loss in molar mass is \(28\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

79.subtopic: Gas Laws and Ideal Gas Equation
79.solution: Gay-Lussac's law states that at constant volume the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, i.e. \(\dfrac{P}{T}=\) constant. Option C states this correctly.

optionOverrides.D: \(P \times V\) = constant at constant temperature and for fixed mass of gas.

80.solution: Sorption is the simultaneous occurrence of adsorption and absorption. When chalk is dipped in ink, the coloured dye is adsorbed on the surface while the solvent is absorbed into the bulk of the chalk, so this is an example of sorption. Charcoal in methylene blue and the gases over Pt/Ni are pure adsorption examples.

81.subtopic: Glycosidic Linkages in Di- and Polysaccharides
81.solution: Sucrose, a disaccharide, gives one mole of glucose (plus one fructose) per mole on hydrolysis. Maltose, also a disaccharide, hydrolyses to two moles of glucose. Hence maltose produces double the quantity of glucose compared with sucrose.

82.solution: Anions B form a ccp array, so the number of tetrahedral voids is twice the number of B atoms, i.e. \(2B\). Cations A occupy \(1/3\) of these tetrahedral voids: number of A \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\times 2B = \dfrac{2}{3}B\).\nRatio A : B \(= \dfrac{2}{3} : 1 = 2 : 3\). Hence the formula is \(\text{A}_2\text{B}_3\).

83.solution: Catechol (1,2-), resorcinol (1,3-) and hydroquinone (1,4-) are all dihydric phenols (two \(-\text{OH}\) groups on the benzene ring). Phloroglucinol (1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene) has three \(-\text{OH}\) groups, so it is a trihydric phenol and is NOT dihydric.

85.solution: Solubility in water depends on hydrogen bonding with water. Alcohols (\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\), \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\)) form strong H-bonds via the polar \(\text{O-H}\) bond; \(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2\) forms weaker H-bonds via the less polar \(\text{N-H}\) bond. \(\text{CH}_4\) is non-polar and cannot hydrogen-bond with water, so it is the least soluble.

86.subtopic: Group 16 Chalcogens, Oxygen, Sulphur and Ozone
86.solution: Conversion of \(\text{O}_2\) to \(\text{O}_3\) is endothermic with \(\Delta H = +142\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), so the enthalpy change for the formation of \(\text{O}_3\) from \(\text{O}_2\) is positive. \(\text{O}_2\) is paramagnetic but \(\text{O}_3\) is diamagnetic (so A is wrong); \(3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{O}_3\) decreases the number of gas molecules so entropy decreases (C wrong); and \(\text{O}_3\) is less stable than \(\text{O}_2\) (D wrong).

87.solution: Tetracyanonickelate(II) is \([\text{Ni(CN)}_4]^{2-}\). Cyanide \((\text{CN}^-)\) is a monodentate ligand with one donor (carbon) atom. With four cyano ligands, the total number of donor atoms is \(4\times 1 = 4\).

88.subtopic: Temperature Dependence, Arrhenius and Collision Theory

89.subtopic: Green Chemistry, Principles, Atom Economy and Green Solvents
89.solution: Water is the ideal green solvent: it is non-toxic, non-flammable and does not generate hazardous waste or pollute the air, unlike chlorinated solvents (\(\text{CHCl}_3\), \(\text{CCl}_4\)). Hence \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) is used to avoid waste and air pollution.

90.subtopic: Galvanic Cells, EMF, Nernst Equation and Thermodynamics
90.solution: The cell reaction is \(\text{Zn}+2\text{Ag}^+ \to \text{Zn}^{2+}+2\text{Ag}\) with \(n=2\). By the Nernst equation \(E_{cell}=E^{\circ}_{cell}-\dfrac{0.0592}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^+]^2}\).\nWhen \([\text{Zn}^{2+}]\) falls from 1 M to 0.1 M (with \([\text{Ag}^+]=1\,M\)): \(E_{cell}=E^{\circ}_{cell}-0.0296\log_{10}(0.1)=E^{\circ}_{cell}+0.0296\,\text{V}\). So the emf increases by 0.0296 V.

91.solution: Chlorobenzene heated with NaOH at 623 K and 150 atm, followed by acidification (Dow process), gives phenol (A). Phenol reacts with bromine water by electrophilic substitution at all the activated positions to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate (B).

92.solution: For N particles in a close-packed structure there are 2N tetrahedral voids and N octahedral voids, i.e. exactly one octahedral void per atom (not per two atoms). Therefore the statement 'there is one octahedral void associated with two atoms' is incorrect. Statements A, B and C are all correct.

93.solution: Solvate (hydrate) isomers differ in the number of solvent (water) molecules inside the coordination sphere versus outside as water of crystallisation. \([\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{Cl}_3\) and \([\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O})_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}\) differ exactly in this way, so they are hydrate (solvate) isomers. Option B is ionisation isomerism, C is coordination isomerism, and D is linkage isomerism.

94.subtopic: Position in Periodic Table and Electronic Configuration
94.solution: An element whose differentiating (last) electron enters the \((n-1)d\) orbital is a d-block element. Among the options, only Ag is a d-block (transition) element; Dy is a lanthanoid and Pu, Pa are actinoids (f-block), where the last electron enters the \((n-2)f\) subshell.

95.subtopic: Position, Electronic Configuration and General Features of d-Block
95.solution: Cobalt (Z = 27) lies in Period 4 and belongs to the first transition series (3d series). Molybdenum (Z = 42) lies in Period 5 and belongs to the second transition series (4d series). Hence the answer is 3d and 4d.

96.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression
96.solution: The rate law \(r=k[\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I}]\) is first order (sum of exponents = 1). The reaction \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I} \to \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{HI}\) involves a single reactant molecule, so its molecularity is 1. Hence both order and molecularity are 1.

98.solution: Entropy increases in the order solid < liquid < gas and increases with more gas molecules. In \(2\text{H}_{2(g)}+\text{O}_{2(g)} \to 2\text{H}_2\text{O}_{(l)}\), three moles of gas form two moles of liquid, a large decrease in disorder, so \(\Delta S<0\). The other reactions all increase the number of gas molecules.

100.subtopic: pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
100.solution: Since \(\text{pH}=-\log_{10}[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]\): at pH 4, \([\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=10^{-4}\,M\); at pH 5, \([\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=10^{-5}\,M\). The concentration changes by a factor of \(10^{-5}/10^{-4}=1/10\), i.e. it decreases by 10 times.

102.subtopic: Section Formula, Concurrency, Foot of Perpendicular, and Distance
102.solution:
The two given lines are \(l_1: 4x + 3y = 10\) and \(l_2: 8x + 6y + 5 = 0\), i.e. \(4x + 3y = -	frac{5}{2}\). Both have slope \(-	frac{4}{3}\), so they are parallel; a line through \(O\) crosses them at \(A\) and \(B\), and \(O\) divides \(AB\) in the ratio of the perpendicular distances from \(O\) to each line.

Distance from \(O\) to \(l_1\): \(d_1 = \dfrac{|{-10}|}{\sqrt{4^2+3^2}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\).

Distance from \(O\) to \(l_2\) (\(8x+6y+5=0\)): \(d_2 = \dfrac{|5|}{\sqrt{8^2+6^2}} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Hence \(AO:OB = d_1:d_2 = 2:	frac{1}{2} = 4:1\).

103.subtopic: Rate of Change and Related Rates
103.solution:
The position is \(x = a + bt - ct^2,\; y = at + bt^2\). The acceleration components are the second derivatives.

\(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = b - 2ct \Rightarrow \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -2c\).

\(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = a + 2bt \Rightarrow \dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} = 2b\).

Resultant acceleration \(= \sqrt{(-2c)^2 + (2b)^2} = \sqrt{4c^2 + 4b^2} = 2\sqrt{b^2 + c^2}\) unit/second\(^2\).

104.subtopic: Vector Geometry — Section Formula, Triangle, and Parallelogram
104.solution: The internal bisector of \(\angle AOB\) lies along the sum of the unit vectors of \(\overline{a}\) and \(\overline{b}\):\n\[\overline{v} = \frac{\overline{a}}{|\overline{a}|} + \frac{\overline{b}}{|\overline{b}|}.\]\nComparing with the given form \(\overline{v} = x\,\dfrac{\overline{a}}{|\overline{a}|} + y\,\dfrac{\overline{b}}{|\overline{b}|}\) gives \(x = 1\) and \(y = 1\), so \(x - y = 0\).

105.solution:

\(P\) divides \(BC\) in \(3:4\): \(P = \left(\dfrac{3\cdot 0 + 4\cdot 1}{7}, \dfrac{3\cdot 1 + 4\cdot 0}{7}ight) = \left(\dfrac{4}{7}, \dfrac{3}{7}ight)\).

\(Q\) divides \(CA\) in \(5:3\): \(Q = \left(\dfrac{5\cdot 0 + 3\cdot 0}{8}, \dfrac{5\cdot 0 + 3\cdot 1}{8}ight) = \left(0, \dfrac{3}{8}ight)\).

Point on \(AP\): \((x,y) = t\left(	frac{4}{7}, 	frac{3}{7}ight)\). Point on \(BQ\): \((1-s, 	frac{3s}{8})\). Equating: \(	frac{4t}{7} = 1 - s\) and \(	frac{3t}{7} = 	frac{3s}{8}\Rightarrow s = 	frac{8t}{7}\). Substituting, \(	frac{4t}{7} = 1 - 	frac{8t}{7}\Rightarrow 	frac{12t}{7} = 1 \Rightarrow t = 	frac{7}{12}\).

Thus \(AG:GP = t : (1-t) = 	frac{7}{12} : 	frac{5}{12} = 7:5\).

107.solution: For \(X \sim B(n,p)\), \(P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}\).\n\[\frac{P(X=k)}{P(X=k-1)} = \frac{\binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}}{\binom{n}{k-1} p^{k-1} q^{n-k+1}} = \frac{\binom{n}{k}}{\binom{n}{k-1}}\cdot \frac{p}{q}.\]\nSince \(\dfrac{\binom{n}{k}}{\binom{n}{k-1}} = \dfrac{n-k+1}{k}\), the ratio is \(\dfrac{n-k+1}{k}\cdot \dfrac{p}{q}\).

108.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
108.solution: The family of lines through \((1,-1)\) is \(y + 1 = m(x-1)\), with one arbitrary constant \(m\). Differentiating: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = m\). Substituting back, \(y + 1 = \dfrac{dy}{dx}(x-1)\), i.e. \(y = (x-1)\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 1\).

109.solution:
Let \(y = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\sin\sqrt{	frac{1+x}{2}}ight) + x^x\) and \(u = \sqrt{	frac{1+x}{2}}\).

For the first part, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}(\sin u) = \dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2 u}}\cdot \cos u\cdot u'\). With \(u = \sqrt{	frac{1+x}{2}}\), \(u' = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{	frac{1+x}{2}}}\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot \dfrac{1}{u}\). At \(x=1\), \(u = 1\), \(\sqrt{1-\sin^2 1} = \cos 1\) and \(\cos u = \cos 1\), so that factor contributes \(\dfrac{-1}{\cos 1}\cdot \cos 1\cdot \dfrac{1}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{4}\).

For the second part, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}x^x = x^x(1+\ln x)\); at \(x=1\) this is \(1\cdot(1+0) = 1\).

Hence \(y'(1) = -\dfrac{1}{4} + 1 = \dfrac{3}{4}\).

110.solution: Equal projections of \(\overline{v}\) and \(\overline{w}\) along \(\overline{u}\) give \(\dfrac{\overline{v}\cdot\overline{u}}{|\overline{u}|} = \dfrac{\overline{w}\cdot\overline{u}}{|\overline{u}|}\), so \(\overline{u}\cdot\overline{v} = \overline{u}\cdot\overline{w}\). Also \(\overline{v}\perp\overline{w}\Rightarrow \overline{v}\cdot\overline{w} = 0\).\n\[|\overline{u}-\overline{v}+\overline{w}|^2 = |\overline{u}|^2 + |\overline{v}|^2 + |\overline{w}|^2 - 2\,\overline{u}\cdot\overline{v} + 2\,\overline{u}\cdot\overline{w} - 2\,\overline{v}\cdot\overline{w}.\]\nThe last three dot-product terms cancel/vanish, leaving \(1 + 4 + 9 = 14\). Hence the magnitude is \(\sqrt{14}\).

111.subtopic: Area Bounded by Curves, Axes, and Lines
111.solution: The parabola \(y^2 = 4x\) and \(y = |x|\) meet for \(x\ge 0\) where \(y = x\): \(x^2 = 4x \Rightarrow x = 0\) or \(x = 4\). On \([0,4]\) the parabola \(y = 2\sqrt{x}\) lies above \(y = x\).\n\[\text{Area} = \int_0^4 \left(2\sqrt{x} - x\right)dx = \left[\frac{4}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^4 = \frac{4}{3}\cdot 8 - 8 = \frac{32}{3} - 8 = \frac{8}{3}\text{ sq. units}.\]\nBy symmetry the region for \(x\ge0\) (with \(y=|x|=x\)) gives this; the answer is \(\dfrac{8}{3}\) sq. units.

112.solution:
With \(	an A = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^2+x+1)}}\) and \(	an B = \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}}\),
\[	an(A+B) =  rac{	an A + 	an B}{1 - 	an A	an B}.\]
Computing the numerator and denominator and simplifying gives \(	an(A+B) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}}{x\sqrt{x}}\).

Also \(	an C = \sqrt{x^{-1}+x^{-2}+x^{-3}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{x^2+x+1}{x^3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}}{x\sqrt{x}}\).

Since \(	an(A+B) = 	an C\), we get \(A + B = C\).
